Summary: Dispensational reading divides history into distinct administrations (dispensations) in which God governs his people in different ways, and it emphasizes the literal fulfillment of Old Testament promises to national Israel alongside a distinct role for the church. Many dispensationalists expect a future literal fulfillment of prophecies concerning Israel, including a millennial kingdom. Covenantal readers disagree, seeing those promises fulfilled in Christ and the church — the difference is a matter of ongoing debate among evangelicals, not of the gospel's core.
HowToApply: Read prophetic promises with attention to their original recipients and terms, and ask whether the New Testament treats a promise as fulfilled, expanded, or still awaiting fulfillment. Let the debate stay where it belongs: on specific texts, not on caricatures of either side.
ScriptureExample: Daniel 9:24-27 — the seventy weeks are read by many dispensationalists as a timeline stretching to a future tribulation and kingdom, while covenantal readers more often see fulfillment in Christ's first coming. Romans 11:25-27 is a shared text both sides appeal to, and it shows why the passage, not the system, must decide.
CommonMistake: Splitting the people of God into two separate plans that barely touch, or forcing every prophecy onto a single timeline regardless of what its own context says.
